utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: A very good morning to everybody. May I ask the registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-02-61-S, the Prosecutor versus Miroslav Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And may I have the appearances. First for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours, counsel. My name is Mark Harmon. I represent the Prosecutor's office this morning. Present with me is Ms. Lise-Lotte Karlsson who is the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I am Slobodan Cvijetic, the Defence attorney of the accused, and next to me is my colleague, my co-Defence counsel, Mr. Slobodan Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And may I finally ask Mr. Deronjic, can you follow the proceedings in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can follow the proceedings and the translation is all right. Everything is fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Deronjic. To start with, I think you can believe that we are not amused that we have to continue with the Sentencing Hearing. In a way it was predicted by the parties that it would support the finding of justice when waiting of -- until the Krajisnik testimony of Mr. Deronjic is over. So let me briefly explain why contrary to our previous decision to be as expeditious as possible what is the purpose of this additional Sentencing Hearing. The Trial Chamber recalls that Miroslav Deronjic pleaded guilty to the Second Amended Indictment and admitted the additional Factual Basis on the 30th September 2003. After his guilty plea and having received some clarifications following his testimony in the present case on 27 January 2004, the Trial Chamber entered a finding of guilt on this basis. The Trial Chamber has seen reasons to de novo review in great detail the Indictment, the Factual Basis, the accused's testimony, his prior statements given to the Office of the Prosecutor, his testimonies in relation to the events in Glogova, only limited to this, given in the case Prosecutor versus Momir Nikolic, versus Radoslav Krstic, versus Slobodan Milosevic, versus Blagojevic et al. The review was in particular focused on the accused's witness statement of 25 November 2003 that was tendered by the Prosecution immediately after the accused's testimony in the Sentencing Hearing in a version that was not yet signed but we agreed that the basis was the B/C/S version, and this B/C/S version reflects what in fact the accused has to say, or wanted to say. As said, this statement and, more important, the accused's testimony in the case Prosecutor versus Krajisnik heard from the 12th through 19th of February, 2004, confirmed the necessity of these additional proceedings. The Trial Chamber has concluded that it appears on a prima facie basis that there are in fact material discrepancies that make it incumbent on the Trial Chamber to verify whether all the prerequisites of Rule 60 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence are fulfilled. I don't want to repeat in all detail what I discussed already the last time. We are only seized with the Second Amended Indictment, and this is only on the events on -- in Glogova in 1992 and the events anticipating these incidents in Glogova. Let me repeat where we have our problems with Rule 62 bis in its application. It reads: "If the accused pleads guilty in accordance with Rule 62 or requests to change his or her plea to guilty and the Trial Chamber is satisfied that the guilty plea has been made voluntarily, the guilty plea is informed, the guilty plea is not equivocal, and there is a sufficient Factual Basis for the crime and the accused's participation in it either on the basis of independent indicia or on lack of any material disagreement, then the Trial Chamber may enter a finding of guilt." In addition to that, also based on the new evidence, these facts have to be discussed. The underlying facts have to be discussed not only in the light of the prerequisites of Rule 62 bis but they might also be relevant as factors for determining an appropriate sentencing. No doubt the above-mentioned prerequisites are in part overlapping and each of the prerequisites of Rule 62 bis have a mutual impact on one another. The Trial Chamber notes that the following statements by the accused alerted the Trial Chamber to check whether the guilty plea by the accused was voluntary. Mr. Deronjic, you pleaded guilty too, and in doing so you admitted the following, and I quote now from the Second Amended Indictment, paragraph 31 through 35: "During the gathering of Bosnian Muslim villagers of Glogova from their homes, members of the attacking forces shot and killed Bosnian Muslim villagers in Delic, Ibisevic, and his wife Zlatija and Adem Junuzovic outside their homes. Miroslav Deronjic is individually criminally responsible under Article 7(1) for committing the killings described in this paragraph." And then I don't want, and I think it's not necessary, the parties know about this in all details. The first mass killing, the second mass killing, the third mass killing are described. May I -- and then in paragraph 4 it reads: "The crimes enumerated in paragraphs 30 through 39 as described in this charge of persecutions in this Indictment were within the object of the joint criminal enterprise and Miroslav Deronjic held the state of mind necessary for the commission of persecution. The crimes enumerated in paragraphs 31 through 34 as described in the charter of persecution were the natural and foreseeable consequences of the execution of the joint criminal enterprise and Miroslav Deronjic was aware that these crimes were the possible consequences of the execution of the joint criminal enterprise." May I ask in this context of Prosecution, we came only across when reading in all detail that in paragraph 4, you refer to paragraph 31 to 34 only. Why is it that you omitted paragraph 35 where it reads: "A total of 65 Bosnian Muslim residents from Glogova were executed during the 9 May 1992 attack. The murdered individuals are those listed in Schedule A which is attached and made part of this Indictment."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have an answer for that. It's certainly nothing that is contested in this case, and I'm quite confident that if we amended the Indictment now that Mr. Deronjic would include in his plea paragraph 35. It is always considered that these number of people were killed in this attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And may I ask the Defence, can we take this as an agreed fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, you can consider this as an agreed fact, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. But now as regards killing, Mr. Deronjic testified in the Krajisnik trial. "At one point I heard that there had been killings and then again this would be denied. It's difficult for me to tell you precisely when it was that I learned that killings had taken place. After the war or, rather, during the war I had the opportunity to read a book in Glogova. This was all done pursuant to my request because we wanted to establish the truth and find out how many people had been killed in Glogova. However, we were not able to get any firm proof, and I accepted the allegation of the Prosecutor, the case of the Prosecutor. Whether this is the exact number, I don't know, but I have no reasons to doubt what they think happened there." This statement has also had an impact on the question whether your guilty plea was in fact informed, i.e., you as the accused have been really aware of the scope and degree of your individual criminal responsibility and that you have -- and that you understood that by pleading guilty to committing persecutions by killings, you admitted you had at that point in time the necessary mens rea. You pleaded guilty to killings. I referred to this beforehand. In doing so, you admitted at the same time during your testimony in -- on page 157 of the Sentencing Hearing transcript, asked by me: "May I with respect to these 65 killings," and you will recall that we heard the names of these 65 dead persons, "that this murder of 65 Bosnian Muslims was the foreseeable result of the attack, and you took into account and accepted that this might happen." Your answer was: "Yes, Your Honour. I stated so, and that the way that is put is correct." End of quote on page 157. The quote started on page 156. The Trial Chamber was primarily alerted whether the guilty plea was not equivocal. Once again, the starting points are your guilty plea and paragraphs 38 and 40 of the Second Amended Indictment where it reads -- I only want to repeat an excerpt, 38: "On 8 and 9 May 1992, Miroslav Deronjic committed and ordered the forcible removal and displacement of Bosnian Muslims of Glogova from the municipality of Glogova [sic]." And then concluding in paragraph 40: "The persecutions of Bosnian Muslim civilians as alleged above resulted in the killings of approximately 65 Bosnian Muslims, the forcible displacement of the Bosnian Muslim population from Glogova and the destruction of the village of Glogova." In the Blagojevic trial, you stated: "I pleaded guilty to the extent it was accepted by the Prosecution that I did not order, that I did not kill, that I was not present, that I did not know of those events but that I was responsible, having ordered the action." And I think the phraseology used was that: "I should have forecast that this could happen. I cannot remember the exact words. I did accept it, and I pleaded guilty to that. I confessed to that." What you have stated in relation to this, that in fact you took into account the foreseeable results and accepted them. I just read from the transcript in this case. Now, you are stating once again in the case Prosecutor versus Krajisnik, on pages 1105 through 1106 of the transcripts there: "I agreed to certain things which I did, but I never agreed to that, nor did I ever order a wish that people are killed. In that period or during the war, I never agreed to anything like that." So we have the development, and this development started already with the statements given to the OTP in the time from June to July 2003 where you said: "I do not consider myself directly responsible for what happened there." I think it's very clear that we need a clarification on these points. Also, the question of material, the absence of a material disagreement between the parties has to be discussed later. Finally, according to Rule 62 bis, the Trial Chamber has the discretion, it reads there: "The Trial Chamber may enter a finding of guilt." What we are doing today is the continuation of the Sentencing Hearing because one thing seems to be clear over all in the world that when the Judges are not satisfied and they are seized still with the case that in fact the guilty plea fulfils all prerequisites set out in the Rules, you can't convict an innocent person. So therefore, we need some clarification. Let me, before going into details of the facts, further details of the facts, I only gave you some examples, proceed with some technical questions. The Trial Chamber, in its order of 19 February 2004, requested the Prosecution to produce the transcripts of the accused's testimony in the Krajisnik trial, and this testimony, the transcript of this testimony were submitted by the Prosecution accordingly. May I ask, are there any objections to admit these transcripts from the Krajisnik trial into evidence in this case? It's not the case. I see nodding from both parties. Thereby admitted into evidence. Mr. Registrar, may I ask you what is the now following JS number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be JS26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Admitted into evidence under this number. Then having read this testimony in the Krajisnik trial, we came across a number of documents, and we requested the Prosecution to produce a number of exhibits tendered in the Krajisnik trial, and nearly everything was produced apart from a document dated the 13th of May that testifies that -- I'm going to quote from Mr. Deronjic: "I expelled volunteers from Bratunac. I have a document about this. The JNA refused to do it, so I did it myself." Prosecution submitted that they are not -- that the Prosecution is not in the possession of this document. The Trial Chamber intends to admit into evidence the following exhibits, and let's go through those that commence case by case, and the deluge of the 700 documents hopefully is melted down to only some documents being relevant for the case before us. I refer to the document, the submission by the Prosecution of exhibits related to testimony of Miroslav Deronjic, and there we can already find the comments given by the Prosecution. First, we have P35. This map shows certain municipalities in which Bosnian Serbs took steps to establish Serb ethnic territories. It's relevant to paragraph 7 and 8 of the Factual Basis. May I ask the Defence, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we come to next document, Exhibit P36 in the aforementioned case. The comment given by the Prosecution is that this document supports the assertion set forth in paragraph 3 of the Factual Basis. It's a decision on appointment of personnel and organisational issues commission: "The Commission of Personnel and Organisational Issues is being constituted with the following members appointed: Dukic Rajko, Karadzic Radovan, Krajisnik Momcilo, Simovic Miodrag, Ostojic Velibor, Neskovic Radomir, Vucurevic Bozidar, Hrvacanin Slobodanka, Jovanovic Jovo, Vukic Radoslav, Bjelosevic Milovan," and then the last one, number 13, is "Sarac Jovan," but the second to last it reads, "Deronjic Miodrag." I know it was discussed already previously, but for the transcript of this case, may I have a clarification, is this just a misspelling or is this Mr. Miodrag Deronjic mentioned there under number 12 the accused in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is a correct spelling from the original document. It was clarified during the trial. This is Miroslav Deronjic. His first name was incorrectly inserted into the original document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can I take this as an agreed fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Agreed fact, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Documents P37, P38 are Prosecution's opinion that these documents appear to be irrelevant to the Factual Basis, and having read these documents, I think it's true. There is no intention to admit these documents. Then we have, and this is the last number of documents or pages, P39 and P40. These documents contain references to, inter alia, the implementation of Variant A and Variant B, phases 1 and 2, are relevant, inter alia, to paragraphs 7, 8, 10, 11 and 12 of the Factual Basis. The then following documents, P41, P42, and so on, they are in part excerpts of P39 or P40. Therefore, it might not be necessary to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. admit both documents in its entirety because then we would admit into evidence the same relevant parts twice. My suggestion would be not to admit P39 but P40, because in P40 there are some parts relevant also for the incidents in Glogova not mentioned in the clips taken in the following exhibits. Are there any objections to admit into evidence document P40 in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we have document P41, the minutes of the emergency meeting of the Presidency of the Municipal Board of the SDS of Bratunac related to the order of the president of the SDS of BH, Dr. Karadzic, where it, inter alia, reads: "Election of the Crisis Staff, number 1, Miroslav Deronjic." And then we have under P42 the minutes of the meeting of the Bratunac SDS Municipal Board held on 25 October 1991. The Prosecution states that these documents corroborate paragraphs 7, 8, 10, 11 and 12 of the Factual Basis and so on, so the relevance is not disputed. Any objections by the Defence to -- in relation to these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then we may turn to document P44, minutes from the meeting of the SDS Municipal Board held on 23 December 1991. The Prosecution states this document supports paragraph 11 of the Factual Basis. Any objections? I can see no. Admitted into evidence. That we have a clear overview, may I ask, Mr. Registrar, later, following the next break, to give copies of the new exhibit list to the parties that we know which document we are referring to later on, now that we have the exhibit numbers, now a concrete case. Then let the document P53, let -- it's the decision that the state of imminent threat of war has been declared the 16th of April, 1992. The Prosecution submits this document is corroborating Factual Basis in paragraph 7. I can see no objection from the Defence. Therefore, admitted into evidence. P54. This document reflects implementation of P53 in the Serbian municipality of Bratunac. It's an order for a general mobilisation. I can see no objections from the Defence. They are nodding, and therefore admitted into evidence in this case as well. Document P55, aerial image, identifies the location of the Hotel Fontana and is relevant to paragraph 15 of the Factual Basis. I can see no objections instead of nodding by the Defence. Therefore, admitted into evidence. Document P56, an order forbidding all paramilitary formations to be active in the territory of Bratunac municipality, and this order is dated Bratunac, the 1st of May, 1992. And the Prosecution has given comments to -- at the same time to the same document, P57, decision on paramilitary formations leaving the territory of Bratunac municipality. This is a document dated 7 May 1992, 1600 hours. I see nodding from the side of the Defence. Therefore, documents P56, P57 admitted into evidence. P61. P61 lists by name a number of Muslims who had been expelled from the Muslim settlements in the Bratunac municipality including the settlement of Suha. According to the Prosecution, it supports the sentence in paragraph 29 of the Factual Basis that Miroslav Deronjic also stated if everything went well with the Glogova operation, the operation to permanently remove Bosnian Muslims would continue in the following days in the town of Bratunac and the communities of Voljavica and Suha. P61, according to the Prosecution, also corroborate's Miroslav Deronjic's testimony on this point. Nodding by the Defence. Admitted into evidence in this case. Then we have finally P63, and this is only in part additional -- of additional relevance and added value. It's a mixture of composition of the 19 December 1991 instructions setting forth Variant A and Variant B. To that end, and this part of the document is already admitted into evidence. However, not the now attached minutes of that very day. So could you accept that we only admit into evidence, not to have the same documents twice, only admit into evidence the minutes of the session of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina of 11 December 1991? Mr. Harmon, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't see the relevance of this document in this particular hearing. This document is eight days before the Variant A and Variant B meeting in Sarajevo. This document was tendered in the Krajisnik case only because of sub-part 2 found in that document as a reflection that Mr. Krajisnik supported the proposition in Variant A and Variant B. Mr. Deronjic did not attend this particular meeting. This particular meeting was separate and apart from anything in this particular case, and indeed it was not -- I don't believe is directly relevant, I say directly relevant to anything in the Factual Basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I hear the Defence on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We agree, Your Honour, with the position of the Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this document needs not be admitted into evidence. The same -- apparently --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I can't check it right now, but I got a message that document P45 was not yet mentioned. These were minutes from the meeting of the Municipal Board held on 24 February 1992. The implementation of level 2 state of emergency where it reads that the suggestion to enter on level 2 state of emergency was unanimously accepted by all the participants. And the Prosecution submitted that this document supports paragraph 12 of the Factual Basis and corroborates the testimony of Miroslav Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So therefore admitted into evidence. I thank you for recalling this. Then we agree with the submission by the Prosecution that the -- the intercept P601 ID recorded in July 1995 is absolutely not relevant for the case before us and therefore it cannot be admitted into evidence. And as in relation to the request to produce the 18th October 1999 documents, the Prosecution correctly states that the already accepted Exhibits P41 and P42 cover this day. So -- and in relation to the 19 December 1999 [sic] Documents, the Prosecution submits that the Prosecution understands the reference to the plural term "documents" in the English translation of the testimony of the accused on the 27 January 2004 to be a reference to multiple copies of the same document. May I ask the Defence, is this correct? Can this be seen as a -- as an agreed fact or are there any other documents of 19th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is an agreed fact, Your Honour. I just draw your attention to the fact that in line 23 it says December 1999. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If it could please be corrected, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's an agreed fact. For December 19th, 1991 document, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And this part of the -- and these instructions are already admitted into evidence under exhibit numbers PS22 and 22A. So finally for the Office of the Prosecutor, may I ask whether the Prosecution is prepared to tender this very interesting map of the area admitted in Krajisnik case as Exhibit P60, 6-0, into evidence, the map of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are prepared to tender it. I have copies in my hand if the assistant could collect them from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And they could be distributed and marked as an exhibit to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Defence has no objection, Your Honour, to this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And may I ask at the same time -- Madam Usher, could you please put this document already now on the ELMO, because we will have to go back to this map for some clarifications later on. May I ask what is the number of this exhibit in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this map would be Exhibit PS40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, 40. Thank you. So then we are -- we have gone through the list of missing documents save one, the document of 13 May 1992. As I already stated previously, the basis for our request was the testimony of the accused in this case, in the Milosevic case where he stated that he is in the possession of a document of this date indicating the expulsion of several -- or at least one individual. May I ask the Defence. Of course, nobody can compel the Defence to produce evidence. Do you want to act?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be -- may I be heard before my learned friend from the Defence on this issue, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can see the Defence agrees, so therefore, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The reason I intervened is because when we received your order requesting the production of that document, I endeavoured to get that document as quickly as I could, and I also consulted with the Defence. As Your Honours know, in two of the documents that are before you, Prosecution Exhibit in the Krajisnik case 56 and Prosecution Exhibit 57, there are two orders, one dated the 1st of May and one dated the 6th of May, both dealing with volunteers, both dealing with actions taken by the Bratunac Crisis Staff to essentially forbid them from actions in the Bratunac municipality. Now, I then sought a production of that particular document through looking through my archives, because it's entirely consistent with not only those two documents but it's also consistent with a document that I subsequently found, a document which you do not have, a document dated the 13th of June, 1992, expelling a particular named volunteer by the name of Nedeljko Sljivanac from Bratunac. He was a volunteer, and he was specifically expelled on the 13th of June. So I consulted with my colleagues and specifically I was informed that this document had been shown to Mr. Deronjic during a proofing session in the Milosevic case. So I then -- and Mr. Zecevic informed me that he specifically recalls seeing that document. I have absolutely no reason to disbelieve Mr. Zecevic when he told me that, so I then searched the archives that I had. I was unable to find this document in my archives. I called the lawyer who was involved in the proofing, Ms. Camille Bibles who is no longer with the Office of the Prosecutor, she's in the United States as a federal Prosecutor, and I asked her about that document, and she recalled that document. So what I can tell you is I'm unable to locate that document. I have other documents that are consistent with that document both before the 13th of May and after the 13th of May. I have a report from Mr. Zecevic that he has seen that document. I have a report from the Prosecutor who was involved in the case and the preparations in the Milosevic case who recalls that document, and I have no explanation as to why I am unable to locate that document. I am -- I cannot. I've searched diligently in my archives, and I can't produce it. That's all I have to say, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe it's even more for the Defence, because it might serve as a mitigating factor, and no doubt there is a difference, and it makes a difference whether this document is now dated the 13th of May, 1992, that is in the four days after the Glogova incident, or the 13th of June, 1992. May I hear you on this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can confirm in full what my learned colleague from -- from the Prosecutor has just stated. This is a fact that we have seen this document dated 13th of May. And my client has seen it, and I have seen it myself. However, the document was produced during the proofing session out of one folder. We saw it. It didn't appear to be necessary for us to have that document because under the instruction of the Trial Chamber at that time, it was -- it was the 9th of May that was the deadline, so we didn't really insist on getting a copy of that document, which is a mistake which we made. Unfortunately, it is impossible, because we tried for two days to locate that document within the archives of the OTP and we couldn't. However, the only thing that the Defence can additionally offer to the Trial Chamber for the corroboration of the existence of that document are the witnesses we have during the preparation of our case. We have interviewed at least two witnesses - one of them Mr. Ljubo Simic, the president of the municipality at that time, and the other person, Dragan Jovanovic, the member of the Crisis Staff - who during our interviews with them confirmed that this decision has been taken, the date, the -- the overall circumstances prior and the reasons why and on whose insistence, I mean the insistence of our client, this decision has been taken by the Crisis Staff. We can -- we can call the witnesses, Your Honour, to that effect if that would be -- if that would be a suggestion by the Trial Chamber. We're -- this is very unfortunately. We understand it's very unfortunate and also from the perspective of the Defence that we cannot produce this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So can we take it as an agreed fact that there exist a document of 13th of May, 1992, where it states that: "I expelled volunteers from Bratunac. I have a document about this. The JNA refused to do it, so I did it myself." It is an agreed fact that a document with this content and fact exists?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. So when turning now, in concretum, to the discrepancies and the issues where the Trial Chamber identified some problems, whether or not the prerequisites of Rule 62 bis are met or not. It's a relatively long list, but consisting in the beginning with some minor clarifications in order to establish the facts prior to the crime. These discrepancies in the beginning, and I want to continue in -- in a timely order, would never warrant a continuation of the Sentencing Hearing. No doubt the core issue before us is the crime as such and its continuation, of course, limited by the Indictment, and there we have two core issues, and this is reflected in our Scheduling Order that one, the mens rea in relation to killings as an act of persecution and the destruction of the mosque. And second, when bringing these thousands of pages together, the picture of the role of Mr. Deronjic remains unclear. Who was finally the responsible person who had the say at these days, the end of April, beginning of May until and through the 12th of May? Was it Mr. Reljic? Was it Mr. Zekic? Was it the accused? And this will be the centre of the discussion, and then some minor issues of the post-crime conduct, once again not warranting as such a continuation of the Sentencing Hearing. I don't know whether or not the parties have already discussed how they want to clarify these issues. The first question, of course, goes, as you can read from the Scheduling Order, to the Defence. Is your client willing and prepared to continue with his own testimony? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we've studied your Scheduling Order, and we've reviewed the document we received, which is called the document of differences, table of discrepancies, and our position in all of this is as follows: The Defence stands by the plea of Miroslav Deronjic who has admitted guilt in this case, as well as his pleadings in respect of the Second Amended Indictment, as well as the Factual Basis which explains the basis for his admission of guilt. Of course we abide by everything that he has stated before the Trial Chamber on the 27th of January of this year. Of course, if the Trial Chamber, in spite of that finds that there are certain distinctions, contradictions or unclear things in his statement, we are prepared to propose one way of proceeding further in this hearing. We would like to suggest that you allow us, as you instructed in your Scheduling Order, that we first, since you instructed the parties to agree on as much as possible, for us then to agree with the Prosecution about the facts that you have mentioned, the ones that we can reach agreement with at least. If in spite of that there are still certain explanations which the Chamber -- the Trial Chamber feels it is owed from us, then we hope that you will allow us to consult with our client and agree on the manner in which he will perhaps augment his testimony before this Trial Chamber. We would first, then, like to agree with the Prosecution in regard to some of the facts that you mentioned, as many as possible, and then after that we would like to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any objections by the Prosecution to proceed this way?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then let us start, as I said beforehand, with some minor points only to establish the entire facts prior to the crime. Let's start with the testimony, transcript page 125 through 126 where Mr. Deronjic stated that -- about events in November 1991. In the Krajisnik transcripts, it reads: "In addition, after meeting of 18 October 1991 in Sarajevo, Miroslav Deronjic held an emergency meeting in the Municipal Board of the SDS Bratunac established by the Crisis Staff. And then another meeting of 25 October 1991, another meeting of Municipal Board, the election of the commission for propaganda and technical assistance accepted by the idea of regionalisation." This is transcript page 927. I think we have already admitted into evidence the underlying documents. Can these two facts that these meetings took place the 18th and the 20th of -- 25th of October 1991, can we take this as agreed facts? I see nodding from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have the exhibit numbers, please, once again to look at those exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Harmon, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have them, Your Honour. They were in the Krajisnik case. They were Exhibits P41 and P42. And we are obviously prepared to accept the contents of those documents and what those documents reflect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. And when I now continue, I always continue with the caveat please understand that in front of this deluge of paperwork there may be the other -- the one or other mistake, so please me -- please correct me if I'm wrong. This is the second issue of minor importance, Mr. Deronjic being a member of the Main Board of the SDS. In the Blagojevic et al. Transcripts it reads on transcript page 6364: "Zekic's death did result in my loaning to the board of the SDS, but only after 1993." Whereas in the witness statement of 25 November 2003 it reads: "I became a member of the Main Board of the SDS in the summer of 1993." In the Indictment and in the Factual Basis it reads: "Miroslav Deronjic became a member of the Main Board of the SDS in summer of 1993." So what is now correct? Only after 1993, as it reads in the Blagojevic transcripts, or in summer 1993? Maybe also here we can proceed on agreed facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think this should be relatively easy resolved. Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, simply in the transcript during the testimony in the Blagojevic case it was just a slip of the tongue. I think we have agreed that this is actually the period of summer 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can we take this as an agreed fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the third issue, Mr. Deronjic and his relation to the War Presidency. In the Milosevic transcript it reads: "In 1992, Miroslav Deronjic was president of the War Presidency in Bratunac." In the witness statement of 25 November 2003, that's the one we have only in B/C/S and not signed in English, it reads: "I was appointed a member of War Commission of the Bratunac municipality." In the Indictment and in the Factual Basis, paragraph 5, it reads: "Miroslav Deronjic was appointed a member of War Commission of the Bratunac municipality." What is now the correct interpretation or what is the correct fact? Was he president or was he a mere member of the War Commission?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Deronjic was a member of the War Commission, and to that effect even the documents exist which we gave to the -- to the Office of the Prosecutor, and I believe that is going to be the agreed fact, that Mr. Deronjic was a member of the War Commission, actually, not the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But could you please explain how it's possible that in the Milosevic transcripts, I refer to transcript page 29735, it states and it reads that: "Miroslav Deronjic was president of the War Presidency in Bratunac. President of the War Presidency was the most important person in that area."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that is a misinterpretation. I really cannot give any better answer than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I hear the Prosecution on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have that knowledge at my fingertips. I need to check that, and I can come back to you after the recess with that if you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I hope not after the recess but after the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. So this remains open. Then the next -- also once again a minor question results from the fact that there are in fact several Crisis Staffs, and sometimes it's not easy to understand which Crisis Staff is meant when it's discussed in the one or other testimony. But the question is now when did Mr. Deronjic become president of the Crisis Staff of the Bratunac municipality? In the Momir Nikolic transcripts it reads: "At 20 something April until mid-June." That's transcript page 104 in that case. In the Krstic transcript it reads: "Towards the end of April, 1992." That's transcript page 135. In the statements given to the OTP in June, July 2003, it reads: "After December 1991 meeting, the meeting about this material was held on the 23rd of December in Bratunac...the first phase. We immediately adopted a decision to form a Crisis Staff. We formed the Crisis Staff...at that meeting or...a few days later...I was elected president of the Crisis Staff." This would be in 1991. Then in the witness statement of 25 November 2003, it reads: "I was president of the Bratunac Crisis Staff...from the end of April 1992 to June 1992." Indictment and Factual Basis states: "An SDS Crisis Staff was formed and Miroslav Deronjic was elected president. A Serb Assembly was established and Ljubisav Simic was elected president of that organ." In the testimony of the Sentencing Hearing, transcript page 131 it reads: "A day or two after the 18 October meeting, they established a Crisis Staff of the Serbian people and Miroslav Deronjic became its president. Upon instructions of 19 December, a second Crisis Staff was set up. Then Miroslav Deronjic became a president of the latter Crisis Staff. The first stage was introduced at once." And then: "At that time," that's transcript page 142, "the 17th of April, I had no executive function in the Bratunac municipality except that I was the president of the SDS Bratunac Crisis Staff." Whereas in the Indictment and in the Factual Basis, and here I refer to the Indictment, paragraph 1, the accused has pleaded guilty to this, it reads: "Miroslav Deronjic was president of the Bratunac Crisis Staff from April 1992 to June 1992." I don't know whether it is possible in light of the many Crisis Staffs to establish when he now exactly became president of the Crisis Staff of the Bratunac municipality and, first of all, had executive functions in the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be of assistance. Actually, the explanation in the testimony of the Sentencing Hearing, transcript page 131, is -- is the explanation which -- which I'm submitting again. So after the October 18th meeting, there was the first -- let's call it the first Crisis Staff of Serbian people was formed, and this Crisis Staff, Mr. Deronjic was the president of that Crisis Staff in Bratunac. This Crisis Staff lasted until the 19th of December, 1991, when an SDS, so the party Crisis Staff, was established. This party Crisis Staff lasted towards the end of the -- and Mr. Deronjic was the president of the party SDS Crisis Staff. Towards the end of April, the Crisis Staff of municipality was formed, and it lasted until June when the War Presidency was established. So the Crisis Staff of the municipality is end of April until June. When it's -- when it's said in Momir Nikolic at 20 something April, it is basically at the end of the April, because Mr. Deronjic cannot recall and we cannot establish exact date when the -- exact date when the -- when the -- when the municipality Crisis Staff has been established, but it is -- it is undisputed that it is the -- towards the end of the April. So on the 17th, there was no Crisis Staff of the municipality of Bratunac. It didn't exist. At that point, Mr. Deronjic was the president of the SDS Crisis Staff. So a second Crisis Staff. I hope I have been of assistance to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Unfortunately, there still remains a problem, because in the testimony at the Sentencing Hearing Mr. Deronjic was referring to a first Crisis Staff of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And he became its president.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But step by step. This is an agreement fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then upon instructions of 19 December, a second Crisis Staff was set up. Then Miroslav Deronjic became the president of the latter. Now we have already two, and he is also the president of this second Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That is the SDS Crisis Staff, party Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We take it as an agreed fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what now about the final problem in the Indictment? Paragraph 1 it reads: "Miroslav Deronjic was president of the Bratunac Crisis Staff from April 1992 to June 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then in the Sentencing Hearing Mr. Deronjic testified: "At that time I had no executive function in the Bratunac municipality except that I was the president of the SDS Bratunac Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we see no discrepancy in the -- between the Second Amended Indictment, paragraph 1, and the testimony of our client. Our client has said towards the end of the April, and the -- the Second Amended Indictment in its paragraph 1 says: "Miroslav Deronjic was the president of Bratunac Crisis Staff from the time when it assumed authority from the Executive Committee of the municipality and the organs of the Municipal Assembly in April 1992 to the time of its transformation to War Commission in June 1992." We do not dispute that it's -- that it's the month of April. The only thing we are saying is that it's towards the end of the April. And the first -- the Second Amended Indictment, its first paragraph doesn't reflect the specific date or the time period or the period of the month which was in -- which the party -- which the Prosecutor is alleging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To facilitate the proceedings, can we take it as an agreed fact that towards the -- as it was the wording now, towards the end of April 1992 to June 1992? This would cover the entire period of the alleged crime, that at that time he was president of the SDS Bratunac Crisis Staff? Can we take this as an agreed fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that has been agreed in paragraph 4 of the Factual Basis where it reflects the end of April. "...From the end of April 1992 to the time of its transformation to a War Commission established by the Presidency of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to June 1992." So that has been agreed upon previously. We are prepared to agree once again to that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like just one clarification, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour just mentioned something which is not correct. The Crisis Staff from -- which existed towards end of April until June is not an SDS Crisis Staff. It is a municipality of Bratunac Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Your client stated on transcript page 142: "At that time, [17th of April]," 1-7 April, "I had no executive function in the Bratunac municipality except that I was the president of the SDS Bratunac Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's -- that's true. And toward the end of the April, ten days or 12 days after that, the -- the municipality of Bratunac Crisis Staff has been formed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Which had the executive power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think then it's clear and -- yes. Towards the end can be read including the 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. We said towards the end, and I said ten days after the 17th of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Now we have the clarification necessary, and may I ask the Prosecution, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's not turn to the next issue, but maybe it's appropriate time for having a break before we then turn to the core issues warranting the continuation of the Sentencing Hearing, but I would kindly ask the Prosecution to come back to the question whether or not Miroslav Deronjic was already president of the War Presidency in Bratunac in 1992 as reflected in the Milosevic transcripts, 29735. The trial stays adjourned until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Harmon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Your Honour. I, during the recess, was able to resolve the question put to me by Your Honour and the other members of the Trial Chamber. I have two documents which I will introduce as exhibits in this case. They are being copied at the moment. I don't have them to tender, but I will momentarily. One document is dated the 16th of June, 1992. It is signed by the president of the Serbian municipality of Bratunac and the republican commissioner, the War Commissioner by the name of Dr. Dragan Djukanovic, and it lists as a member of the War Commission, Mr. Deronjic. The second document I will introduce is a document dated the following day, the 17th of June, 1992, signed by Dr. Radovan Karadzic confirming the members of the War Commission for the municipality of Bratunac, and it identifies Mr. Deronjic as a member of the War Commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you have any idea how it was possible that Mr. Deronjic, when testifying in the case Prosecutor versus Milosevic, stated himself that he was president of the War Presidency in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have not listened to the original B/C/S transcript, the session, so I don't know whether that's an error in translation, whether that is, frankly, a mistake, an innocent mistake by Mr. Deronjic. I can't account for it. I would need to actually listen to the transcript to see if indeed that is a proper reflection of what was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: After having conferred, we come to the conclusion that this point can't be clarified by an agreed fact because we have first to find out whether this was a mistake in the interpretation which -- we have the English version before us, and here it clearly reads -- first the discussion is on 1995, not relevant for this concrete case, but it reads: "But before that you were president of the War Presidency in Bratunac," and the answer is: "Yes, but in 1992." "Question: The president of the War Presidency was the most important person in that area, wasn't he?" "Yes." So this can be clarified in principle by the accused himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Now, coming back to this issue, this testimony was made under solemn declaration, and it's rather difficult to understand that this can be seen as a -- but, of course, everything is possible, but it's rather difficult to explain it as a misinterpretation. So therefore, that what has according to the transcript been said by Mr. Deronjic himself can only be clarified by himself. So this question has to remain open, and we will continue later with this point. When discussing the first part of this morning's hearing, we came across that. Unfortunately, we have to come back to another issue, and this was the question of Deronjic being a member of the Main Board of the SDS. We can take it that it's absolutely undisputed that Mr. Zekic had been killed on the 8th of May, 1992. I see nodding from the side of the Defence. And then in the Indictment and Factual Basis it reads: "Deronjic became a member of the Main Board of the SDS in summer of 1993." The witness statement, summer 1993. In the Blagojevic et al. Transcript, only after 1993, whereas -- and it seems to be consequent in the Momir Nikolic transcripts, and for the court reporter, I will always indicate from now on when I quote and when I am just paraphrasing. I quote now from transcript page 104 to 105. "In the summer of 1992, the party renewed its activities, and I was co-opted as a member of the Main Board because my predecessor Mr. Zekic was and somebody from the area needed to represent the area in the SDS Main Board." In parenthesis I want to add that the word "killed" is missing in this sentence. "My activities were the customary activities of a party at municipal level, so I covered party issues in that area." So the -- there is not only the aforementioned discrepancy, whether it was now only after 1993 but the question, Zekic killed the 8th of May, and Mr. Deronjic's evidence in Nikolic that in -- that he was co-opted as a member of the Main Board because of the death of his predecessor Mr. Zekic. May I ask the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is not a contested fact between the parties. This is the summer of 1993. It is obviously a mistake to have mentioned the summer of 1992. Therefore I don't see any difference between the parties and even in the statements made by the accused himself. As a matter of fact, when Goran Zekic got killed, there was a vacancy there from the area that he had been elected from, but in the summer of 1993, it was Mr. Deronjic who became a member of the Main Board of the Serb Democratic Party, because that is when the party renewed its activity, in 1993, in the summer of 1993, not in the summer of 1992. Mr. Deronjic, in his statements, explained why he in a way froze his political activity precisely in the period of time that you have referred to. He mentioned that he had had a family tragedy, that his wife had committed suicide. So he devoted his -- himself only to his family, and he was not involved in politics. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: However, you will understand that the testimony in the transcript, in the case Prosecutor versus Nikolic, Momir Nikolic, no doubt would make sense when allegedly, and I quote once again: "In summer of 1992, I was co-opted as a member of the Main Board because my predecessor, Mr. Zekic, died and somebody from the area needed to represent the area in the SDS Main Board." So it's once again difficult to understand if there was a need to fill this gap. It would be only consequent to follow his testimony in Momir Nikolic. But may I hear the Prosecutor on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I'm unable to comprehensively give you assistance because I wasn't aware that this was going to be an issue in this case. I can find proper documentation to support, I believe, what has been said by my colleagues from the Defence. I don't dispute one thing said by the Defence at this point in time, and if the Court wants, I will be -- as I said, I will be happy to go back to my office and see if I can find supporting documentation to that fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It would indeed be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: After having conferred, we regard this for the time being as an agreed fact. However, it would be of assistance for the Chamber if you could provide us with supporting material on this issue. Now, let us continue with arming of the Serbs in 1991 and Mr. Deronjic's participation. In the Krajisnik transcripts it reads: " ... In the summer of 1991, as far as I remember," and now it's a quote, "there were already rumours about the arming operations in Bratunac. The secret was out, and pressure was brought to bear by some people who thought that they didn't receive arms, whereas some others did. So I issued orders to distribute those weapons to people who could be trusted to keep it secret. That was necessary, I thought, because there was a danger the police might find out about it and seize the weapons." Transcript page 963 through 964. Can we take this statement also as an agreed fact for the purposes of this case? First the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then let's turn to the next issue. That's implementation of the second stage of the instructions of 19 December 1991. Here we have in the Krstic transcripts a straightforward testimony, and I quote from transcript page 139: "Certain measures...I implemented in the joint assembly in Bratunac. I did implement all the instructions linked to that, and your conclusion is correct." Then in the Indictment and in the Factual Basis it reads: "Late February, 1992, Goran Zekic...conveyed the order to implement the second phase of these instructions in Bratunac municipality, and Miroslav Deronjic took positive and concrete actions including affirmative actions in the Bratunac Municipal Assembly." Mr. Deronjic confessed this as being true in the Factual Basis, paragraph 12. In the Krajisnik transcript, it reads now, I quote from transcript page 1179: "In January we already spoke with Goran Zekic about the implementation of the second stage. A definite, final position to implement this was reached in February 1992." And then: "I even submitted my resignation, not wishing to embark on the implementation of these objectives. I felt that this would lead to war..." "If I carried this out in Bratunac, I could cause the outbreak of war, and I did not want to be the cause of war breaking out in the municipality of Bratunac." So the minor question is when exactly started the second stage, in January or in February, and by whom was the decision -- or who finally made -- made the decision to implement the second phase. In the Krstic transcripts it's absolutely clear: "I did implement all the instructions," whereas in the Krajisnik transcript it now reads: "I even submitted my resignation, and I didn't want to be the cause for war." May I hear the parties on this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Variant A and Variant B was issued on the 19th of December to Mr. Deronjic and to other municipal leaders in the Serbian community. It described both phase 1 and phase 2. That document was a subject of considerable discussion, both phase 1 and phase 2, and I have absolutely no doubt that it was a lively discussion on all elements described in that document. When Mr. Deronjic says he had a discussion with Mr. Zekic about phase 2 of the document, I don't have any reason to doubt that. I think that's entirely likely. And indeed, we have submitted in the Krajisnik case a document, P44, the numbering of the document in the current hearing I don't have at my disposal. I was given a list but I don't have that at my disposal. But the document that is P44 is a document of a meeting held on -- let me get another document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 23 December.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There is a document -- there's two documents. There is P44 which talks about the initial implementation of Variant A and Variant B, and then there is a second document, P45, which talks about the -- receiving to the Bratunac municipal Main Board proceeding to level 2, and I quote: "Deronjic read the material regarding the level 2 which he received from the centre and added that since it was an order, it was our duty to act accordingly." My recollection is that this was described in the testimony of Mr. Deronjic in the Krajisnik case. My recollection is that Mr. Deronjic also said that Mr. Zekic was his conduit of information as to the implementation of phase 2. And my recollection of Mr. Deronjic's testimony in the Krajisnik case as well, he said every particular element of phase 2 described in the 19 December 1992 -- 1991 document was not implemented in the Bratunac municipality, and he explained in his testimony why that was not implemented, and he described what was implemented from phase 2 and what was not implemented in phase 2. So I have -- in terms of the discrepancy mentioned by the Court, I can only say that it is undisputed in this case that Mr. Deronjic received Variant A and Variant B on the 19th of December, that he implemented phase 1 of Variant A and Variant B on the 23rd of December, 1991, as reflected in Prosecutor's Exhibit 44, that he implemented phase 2 of Variant A and Variant B as reflected in the Krajisnik Prosecution Exhibit P45, that not every element of phase 2 was implemented. That's what I can say in respect of Your Honour's concerns about any matters relating to the implementation of Variant A and Variant B in the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So is it seems to be undisputed that the document P45, unfortunately I don't have the exhibit number in our case -- that the measures to implement level 2 state of emergency were accepted unanimously, and the document as such was -- it's not -- its authenticity is not contested, was signed by Mr. Deronjic himself. Can we take this as an agreed fact? Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. At the same time, we subscribe to the explanation that Mr. Harmon gave. So JS33 is the number of the document. That's what my colleague said to me just now. So we agree with what Mr. Harmon said, but I would like to draw your attention to another fact. There are some differences in interpretation in terms of what Mr. Deronjic said as a witness in various cases, and this is due, inter alia, to the fact that in different trials he was asked to clarify details to a different extent. In some trials his explanations were very brief, but elsewhere he gave definite explanations. In this case, we would like to invoke the Prosecutor versus Krajisnik. I think he spoke in the greatest detail there. So we agree with that. There were two levels. Miroslav Deronjic explained what it was. I don't have to repeat it now. He explained Variant B as well, the second level, what was possible in terms of being carried out in Bratunac and what was not. So he explained that in great detail, so we subscribe to what he said, and we have no further clarifications in this regard. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe we have to come back to this in the context of the now following more important issues, and this is about Mr. Deronjic's knowledge of the use of force as part of the plan, and this refers for the first time to the mens rea. In the Milosevic transcripts it reads on page 29752, I quote: "In the beginning of 1991, I understood, however, that the objective was to join Serbia and that it was also planned to use such means as expulsion, killing, et cetera...I'm talking about the beginning." When asked, he continued: "I'm talking about the beginning of 1992." So the emphasis lies with the word "to use such means as expulsion, killing, et cetera." In the Indictment and in the Factual Basis, I quote: "Late February 1992...Miroslav Deronjic subscribed unequivocally to the policy of creating Serb ethnic territories within BiH and later to the use of proclaiming a state of an imminent threat of war, and the second one was a decision on general mobilisation." That's paragraph 96. Thank you for this clarification. I was in the wrong column. "Later to the use of force to remove non-Serbs from Serb designated territories." Factual Basis, page 13. And then in the testimony at the Sentencing Hearing, 27th of January before this Chamber, Mr. Deronjic said: "And today," today, "I know that these violent methods were part of the strategy to create Serb ethnic territories in BiH." That's transcript 133 through 134. Continues by saying: "On the 5th of May, 1992, in a conversation with Mr. Zekic, I found out that beside all the plans which never explicitly contained the use of force, that use of force was planned and that it was already implemented in neighbouring municipalities." Transcript page 134. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. To be continued: "I found out about the use of force before this event earlier, and prior to my conversation with Mr. Zekic...the events began on the 1st, the 1st of April and continued throughout April. During that time, I drew certain conclusions about the use of force in Bijeljina and Zvornik and in some other municipalities about which I found out through the media. The term 'use of force' includes violent transfer of population...conduct of volunteer units...and JNA...The use of arms, the use of a tank...the killing of people."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you're quoting from a transcript it would be helpful to the parties if you could give us the page cite on that, because I followed you through page 134, but I couldn't find the rest of what you were quoting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The last part was 137. "I'm referring specifically to the term 'use of force,'...including the killing of people." May I ask the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm busy trying to find the various passages you're referring to. Could I have -- I didn't hear the exact question you want me to address. I'm prepared to do it, so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So just to repeat the main subject. Already in Milosevic, Mr. Deronjic, explained that: "In beginning of 1991, I understood, however, that the objective was to join Serbia and that it was also planned to use such means as expulsion, killing, et cetera." And then he clarified: "I'm talking about the beginning of 1992." I think we can take this 1992 as an agreed fact. I see nodding from the parties. So therefore, this should be no problem. But then it was confirmed in his own testimony that -- I now refer to transcript page 138 be: "The events began on the 1st of April and continued throughout April...during that time, I drew certain conclusions about the use of force in Bijeljina and Zvornik, and in some other municipalities about which I found out through the media." But then later -- we are referring to a transcript page 137: "The term of 'use of force' includes violent transfer of population...Conduct of volunteer units...and JNA,...the use of arms, the use of a tank...the killing of people."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I'm having difficulty finding the portion that talks about the use of a tank and -- I have seen your reference to the use of force on page 137, and I have found that portion on 134, but I am having difficulty finding the particular portion you just quoted, and I would like to refer to those parts of the transcript before I give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On page 137, I asked the accused: "So it includes the conduct of the volunteer units which had arrived in the area and the JNA; correct?" The answer of Mr. Deronjic: "Correct, Your Honour." "Would it include the use of arms, the use of a tank?" "Correct, Your Honour, yes." "Would it include the killing of people?" "Yes, Your Honour, that's correct. Members of the Muslim ethnic group were killed in that period." But no doubt this has to be read together with the testimony in Milosevic where he -- there was a clear statement without interruption that the means to be used were expulsion and killing, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Harmon, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, you're asking me to explain different testimonies. I wasn't a party to the Milosevic case. I can tell you, however, that it was in April when the violence started in Bijeljina. It was no secret or mystery what happened in Bijeljina. There were expulsions and there were killings. There was cleansing in the Bijeljina municipality, and it followed in a southerly direction in other municipalities. So as these events progressed in the direction of Bratunac, everybody, Serb, Croat, Muslim, and third parties, international observers, and everybody else could see the pattern developing. It was not a mystery. So when Mr. Deronjic testified that he could see this progression coming toward the Bratunac municipality, it makes complete sense to me, and I accept his evidence on that basis. What discussions were had and when discussions were had about the ethnic separation of people I can tell you some things. There were discussions in the -- in the Assembly, the joint assembly, where Mr. Karadzic stood up and said in no uncertain terms that Muslims would disappear. There were discussions and repeated discussions in the Bosnian Serb Assembly that Muslims would disappear and words to that effect. The fact that it was understood by Mr. Deronjic that there had to be a separation of the ethnic groups, that there were going to be -- there would be bloodshed is not a startling revelation to me. Indeed, one of the strategic objectives of the Serbian people -- the first strategic objective promulgated on the 12th of May, 1992, was the separation of the ethnic communities. That was the most important of the strategic objectives, acknowledged to be the most important strategic objectives by Mr. Krajisnik and all other strategic objectives were to be subparts of that principal objective. So when Mr. Deronjic says that it included the removal and the separation of the races, the ethnic groups, to me, Mr. President and Your Honours, given the rhetoric that had started in 1991 in the joint Assembly and the repeated rhetoric that occurred emphasising the same thing, "We can't live together with the Muslims. We can't live together with the Croats. We want to be part of Serbia. We want our own state," that kind of rhetoric clearly is consistent with the testimony of what Mr. Deronjic had to say. Those would be my submissions. If Your Honours have additional questions, I can again provide you with documents identifying those kind of rhetorical comments by responsible members of the Bosnian Serb leadership at the republic level, members of the Assembly, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, but this is not the exact point. The exact point is whether or not Mr. Deronjic at that time had the necessary mens rea to hold him responsible for killings. And Mr. Deronjic pleaded guilty to and confessed the facts included in the Factual Basis, and there it reads: "Late February 1992, Miroslav Deronjic subscribed unequivocally to the policy of creating Serb ethnic territories within BiH and later to the use of force to remove non-Serbs from designated territories." And maybe to facilitate the proceedings, isn't it true that Mr. Deronjic in fact learned already, not only from the objective he referred to in the Milosevic transcript but also from other municipalities in the past that use of force included killings and, therefore, killing was a foreseeable act for Mr. Deronjic also in relation to the events in Glogova the 9th of May, 1992? This was foreseeable, and as he himself stated in his own testimony before us that it was foreseeable. He took this into account, and he accepted these killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, that description of what you have just said is found in paragraph 42 of the Factual Basis, and there is no dispute of what is contained in this Factual Basis. Mr. Deronjic, and I quote, in respect of the killings that took place in Glogova. He: "Did not physically commit any of the murders of the 65 victims in Schedule A. However, at the time he ordered the attack, given the purpose and the objective of the attack, the existing political climate, and the units that were to participate in it, it was foreseeable to him and he was prepared to take the risk that innocent Muslim residents of Glogova would be murdered as it was a consequence that was natural and foreseeable." I don't believe Mr. Deronjic has come off that element of his Factual Basis. I defer to my colleagues from the Defence, but we continue to maintain that that is -- those facts are true and accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The problem only emanates from the facts, and I quoted this earlier, that in a later testimony that was in the Krajisnik case, I paraphrase now, Mr. Deronjic stated that he never agreed to this, that he didn't know about this, that only later he read in a book about this, and he asked the investigators to clarify whether indeed people were killed in Glogova. But this was no doubt after the events, and therefore we have to go into some details whether Mr. Deronjic stands by his testimony in this case, stands by his guilty plea in this case, or whether he -- and maybe he has misunderstood the meaning of all these legal terms, he wants to depart from this what he pleaded guilty to and what he testified before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the Krajisnik case, on page 1243, in cross-examination, Judge Orie asked Mr. Deronjic: "When did you first find out how many people were killed in the Glogova attack." And his answer was: "I never learned the exact number of the people who were killed in Glogova." And he went on to say: "Information about the possibility there have been killings in Glogova, after the funeral of Zekic," the funeral of Zekic, I add parenthetically, was held on the 8th of May, 1992, "...Someone did mention that people had been murdered in Glogova. However, this person, I cannot remember who it was, was not certain about it. In the course of the several following days, I'm sure I did not have any opportunity to become acquainted with this." He goes on to say, starting at line 15 on this same page: "Later after that period different information reached me about the events in Glogova. At one point I had heard there had been killings and then again this would be denied. It is difficult for me to tell you precisely when it was that I learned that killings had taken place." And that was the answer that Judge Orie was soliciting, when did you exactly learn how many people were killed. He then went on to describe after the war, or during the war, he says, there was mention of killings, and he identifies the author of a book, and based on what he learned in the course of his inquiries and information he received from third parties and third -- and other sources such as books, Mr. Deronjic concluded that there were killings in Glogova. He never has disputed that fact before this institution. He has said in his Factual Basis that he accepts the responsibility for that. In terms of any disagreements on that issue, I don't think we have any between the parties, and I don't think we have any in respect of Mr. Deronjic's willingness to stand up once again before this Tribunal and say what is found in paragraph 42.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I -- and I think it's more for the Defence than for the Prosecution to answer these questions. In the statements to the OTP, June, July 2003, and I refer to page 940, I quote: "My role in the events in Glogova is such that I have just described to you. Let me just say this: I do not consider myself directly responsible for what happened there." And in the Krajisnik transcripts: "I agreed to certain things which I did. But I never agreed to that, nor did I ever order or wish that people are killed. In that period or during the war, I never agreed to anything like this." And once again, page 903 of the statements to the OTP: "I told you that I did not feel that I was directly responsible for those people who were executed there." So it's a really difficult question before us, because we are discussing now legal terms, and we have to be satisfied that Mr. Deronjic really understands to what he subscribes and to what he testifies and to what he has pleaded guilty, because when you only learn later from books that people were killed, or from other sources, then it's extremely difficult to establish the necessary mens rea before the crime being committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour has referred to pages 940. My pagination is different. Could you direct me to the day in which Mr. Deronjic said that in the interviews that preceded the guilty plea?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I refer to page 904 of the statements given to the OTP, always with the caveat that they would never -- these statements would never be used against Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, my -- unfortunately, my interview which you have referred to is not paginated and doesn't have 940 pages. My interviews are sequential. They have dates on which the statement was given, and if I could be -- if the date in which that statement was given can be identified for me, I can find it. I would like to see the context in which that statement was given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I refer to the transcript of the interview with Miroslav Deronjic, 9 July 2003. And -- In this interview, it's -- I can only assist you by saying that it's page 15 of 16 it reads.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much. I now have been given copies of these pages that are in accord with your pagination, and I am just trying to find the various references that you have made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The three last -- sorry. The three last lines on page 904. In the bottom line it reads 15 of 16. Here it states: "My role in the events in Glogova is such that I have just described to you. Let me just say this: I do not consider myself directly responsible for what happened there."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I can't get into Mr. Deronjic's head, but let me read on what that statement says, because Mr. Deronjic has always said that he did not directly kill these people who were victims in Glogova. That's part of the Factual Basis. Mr. Deronjic says, and I quote: "My role in the events in Glogova is such that I have just described for you," and what he has just described previously are the murders. "Let me say this: I don't consider myself directly responsible." He said that in the Factual Basis for what happened there. He goes on to say in the following sentence: "However, I deeply regret everything that transpired there, and I especially regret that people, most of them innocent ones, were killed there." So if you're asking me my opinion I think this can be reconciled with the Factual Basis. The Factual Basis is Mr. Deronjic didn't directly kill the people in the village of Glogova. He did, however, order the attack. He did understand that it was -- and it was foreseeable to him and he was willing to accept the risks that innocent people would be killed in Glogova. That is also set forth explicitly in the Factual Basis. I think it's important when we read these various parts of these transcripts, and I will defer to my colleagues from the Defence, but I think these have to be put into the proper context of what else is said in these transcripts. And that is my interpretation, Your Honour, of the reference on page 904 that Your Honour has directed me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let me try to use a very unorthodox way to come closer to a clarification of this point.
