These documents are public, and I think it's important to know, and maybe here the Prosecution can really assist us. The first Indictment confirmed by another Judge of this Tribunal, there was paragraph 23. There was a discussion of the execution of the group of Bosnian Muslims, and then it continues in this paragraph 23: "After the execution of the group of Bosnian Muslims referred to in paragraph 22, members of the attacking forces ordered approximately 15 Bosnian Muslim villagers to carry these and other bodies to the river. Miroslav Deronjic was present near the river bank where Bosnian Muslims' bodies were dumped. At this location a member of the immediate presence -- at this location of the attacking forces executed a Bosnian Muslim villager, Jusuf Ibisevic, in the immediate presence of Miroslav Deronjic." And we can read in the Prosecutor's amended Indictment, in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. paragraph 35: "After the execution of the group of Bosnian Muslims referred to in paragraph 34, members of the attacking forces ordered Muslim villagers to carry these and other bodies to the river. Miroslav Deronjic was present near the river bank where the Bosnian Muslim bodies were dumped. A member of the attacking forces executed a Bosnian Muslim villager, Jusuf Ibisevic, in the immediate presence of Miroslav Deronjic." I take it that these, the first Indictment, and the amended Indictment was based on supporting material, supporting evidence, and we have not to discuss it, but later when there was a Plea Agreement, there was no longer this paragraph and there was no longer, for obvious reasons, the count related to murder. It was no longer charged as murder. So would the Prosecution be in the possession of supporting material that Mr. Deronjic is in fact or was in fact present during the killing, during this second mass killing?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I find this discussion quite uncomfortable. I don't think this is the appropriate place to have this kind of a discussion with the Court. I don't intend to avoid those issues, but to have this public discussion. We superseded this Indictment, both the initial Indictment and the Amended Indictment with a Second Amended Indictment, and the Second Amended Indictment is the instrument that does indeed control this case, and we proceeded on the basis of this instrument. There are many factors that go into a preparation of an amended Indictment and many factors that the Court has recognised. This institution has recognised the value of having cases proceed in a way that is beneficial to the overall objectives of this institution. Those objectives were taken into consideration when this Second Amended Indictment was prepared and accepted by this Court and the plea of guilty on that Second Amended Indictment was accepted. I can -- if Your Honours wish, I can answer some of your questions in a closed session, but at this point in time, that is what I have to say in respect of this Second Amended Indictment, it being the viable instrument on which we are proceeding today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe it's now for the Defence to discuss it, and maybe it really can facilitate bearing the last words of Mr. Harmon in mind. Does your client stand by his testimony before us, and does he stand by the guilty plea and the confession that he admitted that those facts contained in the Factual Basis were correct, or does he contribute that what he said in the Krajisnik case, that he never agreed, that he never was present, that he never knows -- that he never knew about killings at that time? Because one thing is that of course the Prosecution can, when leave is granted by the Chamber, and this was granted, can drop the one or other charge. But nevertheless, we have to come to the truth as close as possible. And in case the Prosecution is in the possession of documents supporting the fact that Mr. Deronjic was actually present during these killings, then it would no doubt be the easiest way if we now hear from the Defence in order to avoid further orders of producing evidence and in order -- maybe we can, by doing so, avoid an additional testimony, but this has to be discussed by the three of us beforehand. Just to clarify, not in legal terms but in terms that are easily understood as well by the accused, that in fact he had the necessary intent of committing persecutions by killings. Of course not by own hand but through others.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, I would like to stress the following supporting the position of Mr. Harmon: When we discussed following Deronjic's admission of guilt, in view of the only act at that point that had legal weight at the time, that is the Second Amended Indictment and nothing else. He was informed. You also informed him of the Second Amended Indictment, not the first one or the one afterwards which you mentioned. We did not discuss that. The Prosecutor, had they not changed the Indictment, there would be no admission of guilt. So now you are making us discuss something that was not the subject of the admission of guilt of our client. I don't see what the problem is right now. Before the break when I proposed the methodology of our work, I suggested that we should make quite clear these facts, together with the Prosecution, that we should agree on these facts that you are pointing to, namely, searching for the true form of the culpability of the accused, his mens rea when we're talking about the killings, and in view of all of that you have quoted just now and which is not in dispute, because Miroslav Deronjic simply stated the facts and events which took place in his immediate vicinity. Stating those facts and even knowledge that in the neighbouring municipalities killings took place does not mean that Miroslav Deronjic would personally commit or order for something like that to happen in Bratunac. However, our client pleaded guilty for the -- for the fact that the murder of 64 innocent civilians occurred. This is just a contradiction, an apparent contradiction which actually does not exist. Searching for a formula which would be adequate to the state of his mind, his mens rea, you, Your Honours, have a coordinated, balanced position of the parties, the Prosecution and the Defence. It is formulated in paragraph 42 of the Factual Basis, which states: "Miroslav Deronjic did not physically commit any of the killings of -- personally of the 65 civilians as cited in appendix or Annex A. However, at the time of ordering the attack on Glogova, in view of the purpose and the objective of the attack, the existing political climate, and the units that were to participate in the attack, it was foreseeable to him and he was prepared to take the risk that innocent Muslim residents of Glogova could be murdered as it was a consequence that was natural and foreseeable." Your Honours, this is the mens rea in the way that we described it, and in this way Miroslav Deronjic admits his guilt to what has happened. This is something that the parties are not disputing. I don't know what else could be under dispute, and I ask you to please help us to elucidate that. Just one more thing, Your Honour. I apologise. In the introduction, I still -- when I spoke about the Second Amended Indictment and the other Indictment, I would like to say just one more thing which I didn't say. It is not incidental that in the Second Amended Indictment a part has been left out which refers to the alleged presence of Miroslav Deronjic when the corpses were thrown into the river. While we were coordinating our position, we told the Prosecution, we presented to them irrevocable evidence that this is not true and that at the time he was not present. We can do that again at a closed session for the Trial Chamber, although we believe that this is unnecessary, because we are discussing the Second Amended Indictment in which this paragraph does not exist. This is as much as I wanted to say for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe -- of course, the Trial Chamber in its entirety has to discuss how to proceed. We still are in the same situation that once in the Sentencing Hearing Mr. Deronjic testified that he took into account and accepted that the killing of 65 Bosnian Muslims was a foreseeable result of the attack and that he accepted that this might happen. There would be no problem at all if there wouldn't be the Krajisnik transcripts, and once again I refer to Krajisnik transcript, page 1105 to 1106 where Mr. Deronjic stated: "I agreed to certain things which I did. But I never agreed to that, nor did I ever order or wish that people were killed in that period or during the war. I never agreed to anything like this." And then of course paraphrasing in other parts, in the Blagojevic trial and also in Krajisnik, he stated that he not even knew about the facts, about these facts. And in order to support this testify -- this testimony, for example in Blagojevic when he said: "I didn't know of these events." He said: "I was several kilometres away from Glogova at that time fulfilling a specific task." That's transcript page 6365 through 6366. Whereas in his testimony in the Sentencing Hearing, he stated that it was about one kilometre away. We are now in the difficulty, and therefore -- in another testimony he stated that it was possible to hear what happened in the town because they were that close to the town, and he heard shooting in the town. But I know that counsel, of course, can't testify on this, so we must consider during the next break what now to do with this, whether it can be clarified by a -- by an unequivocal statement on the mens rea not in legal terms but in a way Mr. Deronjic likes to express his state of mind at that time. I am afraid we can't go further with this right now, and -- yes. Mr. Harmon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, again I'm -- Your Honour is citing for the first time various cites in the various transcripts. We haven't had time to look at those before coming into Court, so it's difficult for us to respond in an effective way. But I will -- I did take the first portion of the citation that you gave us, pages 1105 and 1106. When I examined Mr. Deronjic on the 18th of February, Mr. Deronjic said in his testimony, and I'm quoting in part what you quoted: "I believe, even though I ordered the action of Glogova, even though I participated in it in the way that I described, I agreed to certain things which I did, but I never agreed to that, nor did I ever order or wish that people are killed." We have no evidence that Mr. Deronjic ordered people killed, and indeed in the Factual Basis that is before Your Honours to support this plea, there is no suggestion that Mr. Deronjic, in fact, ordered those killings. The contrary is what is contained in the Factual Basis. So again in respect of this particular transcript, I do not see any inconsistency with the Factual Basis, and that's what causes me some concern in terms of this particular concern of the Trial Chamber. If the Court wishes, and if the Court would give us the opportunity and identify for us the various transcripts of the -- that it is concerned about and finds differences in, we, both parties, I on behalf of the Prosecution, my colleagues from the Defence, can address these in a systematic and coherent way that will be quite expeditious. But -- I can make that suggestion in desiring really to help Your Honours with the problems it has identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. The Defence completely agrees with what Mr. Harmon has said. Actually, when I'm looking at the transcript, the portion of the transcript that Your Honour cited that, I see that it is completely out of the context in which you are referring right now to us, because the question that was posed to Mr. Deronjic was -- I'm citing the Krajisnik 18th of February, 2004, page 1105. The question was: "In respect of the Muslim civilians from Glogova in your testimony, you described they were put on various forms of transportation and moved to Kladanj, which was Bosnian Muslim-held territory. My question, Mr. Deronjic, is: Why weren't these 400 detainees put on a bus and sent to Kladanj? Why were they sent to Pale?" And then Mr. Deronjic gives the answer that you cited. So what they are talking about is actually the incident in hangar, the 400 people that has been transported to Pale in order to be saved from the hands of the volunteers. And in reference to that question is the answer of our client. Thank you, Your Honour. I mean, in that respect, I fully agree that we should be given the opportunity to give our presentation in order to assist effectively this Trial Chamber. I mean, to put the discrepancies in a context where they appear. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just to clarify your own quote, and I quote now from page 1106, line 3: "I believed even though I ordered the action on Glogova, and even though I participated and so on, I agreed to certain things, but I never agreed to anything like that," and here he referred to the killings. So would you yourself establish a link between the events and the hangar and in the stadium of Bratunac and the events in Glogova? Because here it clearly states: "Only I ordered the action on Glogova." And then the question remains -- we have to see everything in context. When your client has then declared, when he was aware what happened in the other surrounding municipalities and this ended up finally with killings, and previously I quoted that from the beginning -- already in the beginning of 1992, the use of power meant expulsion, killing, et cetera. Milosevic transcript. Is it absolutely clear that when ordering such an attack that it was foreseeable that people would not only be expelled but also some of them killed as your client himself confessed?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is not intention, of course, to -- of the Defence to connect the two. I'm just referring to the context of the question and the answer, nothing else. I'm not making any connections between any other events but the event which we are talking about and that is the attack on Glogova on the 9th of May. That is the issue as we are concerned and as we understand. In order to -- to answer your question, I can only revoke the contents of the Factual Basis, paragraph 42, which my colleague already cited. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. We will discuss this issue later if not Mr. Harmon has an immediate solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I which I did have an immediate solution, Your Honour, but I do -- I would like to put that particular answer on page 1106 indeed into context, because if you start at page 1101 of the transcript, this whole discussion between 1101 and 1106 deals with killings in the Vuk Karadzic school, and that's the context in which Mr. Deronjic, the way I read this at least, Mr. Deronjic says, "Look, I ordered the action on Glogova and even though I participated, I agreed to certain things." You know, he goes on to say, "Nor did I --" and he says, But I never agreed to that, nor did I order or wish that people are killed." And this was in the context of killings in -- for a period of days that took place of people who were detained in the Vuk Karadzic school. That's where I see a selected reference to a sentence out of context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Out of context. This is the word I just wanted o use myself, because the problem in this case emanates from the fact that the Prosecution, and the Prosecution no doubt in a party-driven procedure is free to decide what they charge and what they don't. The problem is that we have before us the plan to take over the municipality of Bratunac, and then the Indictment is limited to only the first events in Glogova and only to the 9th of May, and this causes really problems, because when you go into details, we will find out that it's very difficult to identify why you just stopped immediately after the events in Glogova, whereas the more serious crimes apparently and according to the testimony of Mr. Deronjic himself were committed later in -- in Bratunac and that there is indeed a link between these events. For example, when you read the list of the detainees brought from the stadium to Pale, that n this list you identify persons coming from Glogova. And therefore, our problem is here that we are seized with Glogova only, but the events of course continue, and we don't have the slightest gist on what happened with the population of Glogova in its entirety. Were they all brought to Kladanj? Were they brought in part to Bratunac? So this remains open. And I could come back. We have several contradicting statements Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. also on this point, but I wanted -- or at least I try to focus on the core issue, and this is the mens rea for killing. And let's see how we can resolve this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can answer two of your concerns, Your Honour. The first concern is this -- this is indeed a limited Indictment. It was purposefully done so because, among other things, this institution has had trials that have lasted more than two years. Indeed, I participated in one of those trials, and we could have a huge trial on a case that can be resolved very quickly on facts that are clearly provable in this case. So a decision was made by me to limit this Indictment for purposes of resolving this case quickly in order to fulfil the mandate of this institution. The choice being we could have a 25-month trial on this, which would consume huge resources and limit the number of cases that are heard before this institution, or the Prosecutor using her discretion can limit the case to very serious cases, I might add, that are provable and can be resolved expeditiously. That is why that choice was made in this case. In respect of what happened to the people in Glogova, that is mentioned in the Indictment itself and/or in the Factual Basis. Now, if you give me one moment, I will find it. But result of the attack on Glogova, it's either in the Factual Basis or in the Indictment, was that no Muslims remained in Glogova after the 9th of May. They were ethnically cleansed from Glogova. A substantial number of the buildings were destroyed by fire. The mosque was destroyed by fire. 65 Muslims were killed. And indeed as Mr. Deronjic -- as this Plea Agreement says and the Indictment says, that if the attack on Glogova was successful, there was going to be additional ethnic cleansing in the villages of Suha and one other village, and that evidence has been presented to you in the form of a list of people that include people from Glogova who were ethnically cleansed. It includes people from Suha, from Voljavica, the other municipalities that have been identified in this Indictment. Our proof in this case is that at the conclusion of the events on -- following the attack, there was nothing virtually left of the village of Glogova. It was gone. It was no longer for all intents and purposes -- it was not a Muslim village any more because the Muslim villagers had been removed. So in terms of what happened there, this attack resulted in the elimination of that village as a viable community. So those are two answers I hope will help you understand why this is a limited Indictment and will assist you in understanding the consequences of this attack that are not, by the way, in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As I said before, and it's of course only up to the Prosecution to decide where the limits of an Indictment are, and I don't want to go into further details. I only wanted to explain the difficulties when confronted with only a part -- when you have the entire plan being part of the Indictment and then the consequences only limited to Glogova and reading in all testimonies that this was continued later. We are not seized with that what happened later save the meeting in Pale. However, it creates problems when we identify that citizens of Glogova were not in its entirety brought to Kladanj but in part to -- first to Bratunac and then later to Pale. But I think it's now the time and the appropriate time that we have a break for one hour. This leaves us the possibility that we can conclude today only for a better explanation when we have twice 90 minutes, we could then conclude at 5.00 o'clock today, hopefully finally conclude. Let's try to do our very best. The trial stays adjourned until half past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.32 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: After having conferred, may I ask the parties, can we take it as an agreed fact that the accused stands by his guilty plea and his confession, or admitting the Factual Basis, and the -- his testimony in Krajisnik and his prior statements given to the Office of the Prosecutor have no impact on this; and therefore, for both parties, there is nothing equivocal in these statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes. It is just that we are going to add a testimony that was heard before this Chamber on the 27th of January this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I agree with Your Honours' proposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Then the direct thread of the now-following issues is more or less a question of the mutual responsibility of Mr. Zekic, Mr. Reljic, and Mr. Deronjic. Let me start with the question of the disarmament of the population in Glogova. In his witness statement of 25 November 2003, Mr. Deronjic stated: "Between the 28th of April and early May, they" - in the meaning Reljic JNA unit - "started planning and implementing the campaign of disarming Muslim villages in Bratunac. In one such operation, Miroslav Deronjic took part "as an ordinary soldier when the suburb... Podcaus was disarmed. These operations... were conducted until the 6th of May and they included the villages of Glogova, Konjevic Polje, Voljavica." And then in the indictment and in the Factual Basis, it reads: "An effort to disarm was completed by the end of April 1992." That's paragraph 20. "And the disarming continued until 6 May 1992." That's the Factual Basis, paragraph 22. This is only a minor issue. What was it now? Was it completed by the end of April 1992, as it reads in the Indictment, paragraph 20, or continued until 6 May 1992, as it reads in the Factual Basis, para 22? I think this can be easily resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I believe what is more accurate is the factual basis, paragraph 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Agreed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It is an agreed fact that the disarmament took place on the 6th of May 1992. Then, one more-difficult issue is the issue of participation of volunteers. In the statements given to the OTP between June and July 2003 - I refer to page 913 [sic] - it reads: "Army participated and they had their commander. The TO participated with their detachments and they had their commander. The police participated as well, Chief of Police Milutin Milosevic was their superior. Volunteers participated and they had their commander of their unit. I said that I would coordinate the operation, that I would monitor and coordinate the operation." In the testimony at the sentencing hearing, 27 January this year, Mr. Deronjic testified, transcript page 144: "I gave the order to attack the Bratunac TO, including the police forces in Bratunac. I was unable to command the JNA units." Continuing on page 144 to 145: "None of these volunteers attended the Crisis Staff meeting, and my decision stands in relation to them. I don't know to what extent. I don't know what they did participate in this action in Glogova." In the Indictment and in the Factual Basis accepted by the accused, it reads: "Later the same day [8 May], at 2200 hours, the Bratunac Crisis Staff met the principally about the events surrounding the death of Zekic and the operation to attack Glogova. Miroslav Deronjic presided over this meeting. The portion of the meeting dealing with the attack on Glogova was attended by members of the Crisis Staff, Reljic, Rasa Milosevic, Commander of the Kravica Detachment of the TO, and another individual who was a member of the State Security of Serbia." That's Factual Basis paragraph 28. So the first question would be, did now the volunteers participate in the meeting of the Crisis Staff at that very 8th of May or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I believe the Factual Basis, again, accurately reflects what happened. They did not participate in the meeting of the Crisis Staff. That is the information that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Agreed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Take it as an agreed fact. Then in the Krajisnik transcript it reads, testimony of

utterances.speaker: MR. DERONJIC
utterances.text: "I came to a decision that the village of Glogova, that is, that the population of the village of Glogova, should be forcibly resettled from the area. I made this decision on that night at the Crisis Staff without having received prior directives to that effect. I likewise never asked any guidelines for the implementation of this directive, save for the consultations that I had with Goran Zekic and also with Predrag Spasojevic. I received the approval from Mr. Zekic." This brings me to the question, what is now the relationship between Mr. Zekic and Mr. Deronjic, who was, in principle, superior?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Zekic at the time of the -- prior to his death and at the time of the meeting that he had with Mr. Deronjic on the 5th of May in the Hotel Fontana was a member of the Bosnian-Serb Assembly and a member of the SDS Main Board. He was the link to Mr. Deronjic, who was a leader in the Bratunac municipality. That is the relationship between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This was the first question. The second question, we had it already, was a question on the issue of disarmament. In the testimony on the Sentencing Hearing, as well as in the Indictment, it reads: "I gave the order to attack the Bratunac -- to the Bratunac TO, including police forces in Bratunac." "I gave the order." Whereas in Krajisnik, it reads: "We just gave our approval at the meeting." Transcript page 1244 through 1245.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The issue, Your Honour, I think is addressed in paragraph 29 of the Factual Basis, the last sentence. And it indicates that following the introductory marks, again, at this particular meeting, in a discussion of the Glogova plan, the Bratunac Crisis Staff adopted the plan. That is what occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. We agree to that. And even more, in the transcript which you cited, it says: "Yes, one final question for you: The preparation for the attack on Glogova, as far as logistics were concerned, was that prepared prior to the decision taken, or was it organised on all the same evening?" "It was prepared before. The army carried out the preparation. We just gave our approval at the meeting." So it refers to the logistics preparation of the attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it doesn't disturb --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- the fact that Mr. Deronjic gave the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as the President of the Crisis Staff, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then it has to be one minor issue, as I already mentioned before in Blagojevic, at earlier transcript, it reads on page 6365 through 6366 that -- what we already discussed, I didn't know of those events, and so on. But then, I quote: "'If you mean the village of Glogova, when you say the scene, that's not quite true. I was several kilometres away from Glogova for fulfilling a specific task.'" Was it now several kilometres away or was it 1 to 2 kilometres away? Maybe we can avoid testimony by Mr. Deronjic himself when the parties agree in pointing on the map being now on the ELMO where exactly Mr. Deronjic stood at this point in time. If the usher could be so kind, and if there is another copy of the map. I'm afraid Mr. Deronjic has no map, so if you could be so kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I can assist with a clarification. We introduced this map into evidence that was reduced by the Prosecution to an acceptable format. And we compared yesterday this military map that was now placed on the ELMO. On the military map that we are looking at now, the old road going through Glogova village was drawn in. If we place this map onto the old photo, then you see that it doesn't coincide. There is a discrepancy and it goes 90 degrees towards the old road. Mr. Deronjic said he spent the night on that day near the old field and you can get a picture if you compare these two maps. This road is an old macadam road that is no longer being used because a new asphalt road has been built since then. And Mr. Harmon drew a line to mark it in a nice pen. We can get an answer by comparing the two maps briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you could please continue that we have now a map before us. I take it that when -- according to his testimony, once he said "several kilometres, once he said "1 to 2 kilometres," then it should be on this map we have before us. Correct? And if you could be kind enough --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I can assist you here because I walked that entire road that was covered by his unit back then. Let me just tell you. The distance from Glogova village is different because that road is winding. In spots, you are only 1 kilometre away from Glogova, but in other places, the distance is 3 kilometres. I walked the entire road, and the distance varies. But I measured the distance from Glogova at the place where he came out. It's 5 kilometres. So our answer is that we can stipulate an average distance but we can never say exactly whether it's a kilometre or three, because the distance varies due to the winding nature of the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Absolutely. But could you please cross-mark on the map the place where Mr. Deronjic stood at -- in the morning time of the 9th of May 1992, that we -- unfortunately, we are not under -- have not the possibility to be on the crime site to see whether and what he was able to see. But if you could mark it, please, on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, then I would kindly ask to be given DS20. And on that map from 1990 we can show you the position of the road. Because this map that we have now is an old one, and it no longer reflects the exact situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the Registrar, please, to present this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, how do you want it done, physically? Do you want me to place it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In yellow -- I'm not sure the Judges can hear me -- in orange actually, we see the marking of the new road. Above it, you can distinguish this line white line and that is the old road you can see on the military map. Can you see it? That's the old road seen on the military map. The orange line represents the new road, the current situation. Miroslav Deronjic was above this old road. I'm showing the position here. And in the morning, he went down to the old road and moved along the old road to Avdagina field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please cross-mark --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I haven't got my headphones on. I can hear you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please cross-mark the place where Mr. Deronjic stood.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will also mark the place where he emerged on to the road. In the morning hours, he went down to the old road. I marked it with an arrow. Can you see it now? He spent the night where the cross is. In the morning, he went down to the road and moved down the road to the place which I marked with an X. And generally speaking, I followed this road before Glogova. Here is where the two join. There is a marking. He went to the hilly, wooden part, and came out on the road towards noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As he explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, can we take this as an agreed fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, that's satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's admit this document with the marks on it as DS20/A-1. Thereby admitted into evidence. Thank you for this assistance and clarification. To continue with the overall role of Mr. Deronjic. In the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Indictment and in the Factual Basis it reads: "Mr. Deronjic coordinated and monitored the attack." "Mr. Deronjic urged Captain Reljic to fire a tank shell into a house." Then later, in the testimony at the Sentencing Hearing, Mr. Deronjic stated on page 147 and 154: "I did not issue an order. I made a recommendation" -- that's now in relation to torching. But my first question would be on the one-hand side, it reads in the Factual Basis, paragraph 35, that "Mr. Deronjic urged Captain Reljic to fire a tank shell." On the other hand, in the Krajisnik transcript, it reads on page 1.047: "Reljic claimed himself commander of the town. After he, Reljic, took over control, from that point on he was issuing commands to the TO for the mobilisation," and so on and so forth. May I take it that the accused stands by that what he has pleaded guilty to and what he confessed in relation to the Factual Basis, that he urged Captain Reljic to fire a tank shell into a house? Of course, you can't testify about the role but it serves as an indicia on the question who, in fact, had power in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we can assist. What is written in the Factual Basis, we accept as both accurate and as the explanation that Miroslav Deronjic gave on the 27th of January before this Trial Chamber. If this is not enough for the Trial Chamber to make a conclusion, then we can discuss it further, although we believe what is written is precise enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the Prosecution also agrees with this explanation that we have it as an agreed fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then let me turn immediately to the meeting in Pale. I don't want to go into details --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The meeting in Pale, the 10th, 11th, or 12th of May we have it in part in the Indictment, in part in the Factual Basis. In the Indictment, it reads that it was held either the 10th or the 11th of May 1992. In the Witness Statement of 25 November 2003, on the one hand it reads about a meeting held on 12th May in Pale, "when I explained the events on Glogova." That's paragraph 67. And then, "What I saw when I returned from Pale, which was either the 11th or the 12th of May." But then on the other hand, it reads in paragraph 106, "On either the 10th or 11th of May 1992, I travelled to Pale to attend a meeting to report about the events in Bratunac municipality." I don't want to confuse this, but I only want to highlight first the statement as 12th of May and reporting about the events in Glogova, and then 10th or 11th of May, reporting about the events in the Bratunac municipality. If I take the testimony of Mr. Deronjic at the Sentencing Hearing then it's very difficult to understand how it's possible to report already on the 10th of May about the events in the Bratunac Municipality in its entirety. So may I hear the parties on this question. What was the report? Was it the report on Glogova, and then the 12th, or was it the report on Bratunac, the 12th? And finally, and in this context already, in order not to come back to this, that finally it was said by Mr. Ostojic, "Now we can paint Bratunac blue." This would mean the Bratunac municipality. Then at least the 10th would be excluded as the concrete day. Because according to the testimony of Mr. Deronjic during the Sentencing Hearing, it seems to be absolutely impossible what he told us about all the events happening going to -- several times to Bratunac, back, the funeral, looking about -- looking on the crime sites and so on. So the question remains: What was the day and was the report on Glogova or was it the report on Bratunac municipality? Can we resolve it also by the way of having agreed facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, as to the exact date, whether it was the 11th or the 12th, I can't say for certain. I don't think Mr. Deronjic knows for certain. I accept the fact there was such a meeting. In respect of what was reported, I refer Your Honours to the testimony in the Krajisnik case, page 1199 starting at line 24. And there is a summary of what the report was, specifically, the summary that is described by Mr. Deronjic in that testimony -- I'll read his answer: "I said that the population of the village of Glogova had been forcibly moved out. I'm not sure I used the exact expression, but it was perfectly clear that they had not left on their own, of their own free will, that the village by and large had been burned down, that there had been a lot of destruction in Glogova as well, that the operation of the forcible removal of the Muslim population would continue the next day in Bratunac and the neighbouring villages. That was the essence of my statement."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. And this creates the confusion. Because no doubt when he reported already about the events in the entire municipality, then I think all of you can agree that the 10th is not possible as the date. And I wonder how it is possible that in the accurately drafted statement of 25 November 2003 it clearly reads "the 12th of May in Pale."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can't give Your Honours any precise date. I think Mr. Deronjic gave an estimation as to the approximate date. He gave that in his Factual Basis in paragraph 45. He's given a range obviously, with the other testimonies, he says the 10th or the 11th and in other testimony he says the 12th. I make no excuses for Mr. Deronjic, I merely point to the human factor of trying to account for a particular event that took place in 1992. When asked about it in 2004, it's difficult to precisely identify the date. I don't have any dispute nor do I think Mr. Deronjic disputes that this meeting took place. I think there is a question as to the exact date, and I can't shed any additional light on it, Your Honour. I have no additional documents that can help the Court in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then we take it that the Witness Statement of 25 November 2003 where it reads "the 12th of May in Pale" signed in B/C/S by Mr. Deronjic, that might be a mistake. And we take it as agreed facts and the accused stands by his guilty plea in relation to the Indictment and his confession to the Factual Basis. Can this be seen as an agreed fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The paragraph 45 of the Factual Basis is what we stand by. Let me just briefly explain in two words. If Your Honours remember, Mr. Deronjic testified before this Trial Chamber and in other cases also that he was summoned to the meeting. So it wasn't him who chose when to go, but was summoned to go to Pale to report on the situation in Bratunac municipality, as it stands in paragraph 45 of the Factual Basis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank you. The final point I wanted to address relating to certain discrepancies was already discussed this morning and we agreed already that there in fact is a document dated the 13th of May on the expulsion of volunteers from Bratunac. In the statements to the OTP of June, July 2003, it reads: "We decided in mid-May to expel him from Bratunac." This was in accordance with two documents of the beginning of May or mid-May we have admitted into evidence this morning. Then in continues on page 1172: "He was informed about this" decision to expel "so he escaped from Bratunac." So the question, once again: Does this statement given to the OTP that he escaped has any impact casting doubt on his own testimony that he expelled all volunteers from Bratunac? And also a decision to expel Reljic, that was the testimony of Mr. Deronjic, page 164 to 165 the 27th of January, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It doesn't contradict. If I would just briefly explain. The passage -- the part of the statement which you just read explaining the escape, "he escaped" refers to Captain Reljic, not to the volunteers. And therefore, there is no discrepancy. They expelled the volunteers as one measure; they expelled Captain Reljic. But they couldn't expel him because he fled because he found out that he has been expelled. That is the explanation, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So one should read the testimony in the hearing, because there is a reference to a decision to expel Reljic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as a second decision. There is the first decision to expel the volunteers, and then the decision to expel Reljic as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But it was not possible because he escaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's exactly right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can we take this as an agreed fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You can, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank you. Are there any additional questions from your side? So, then, may I ask the parties, are there any additional submissions to maybe discrepancies? I guess that there are none. You assisted us in -- please, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. This morning Your Honours had a question about the War Commission and whether Mr. Deronjic was a president or a commissioner, and I have two documents which I referred to I can now pass up to Your Honours as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We already discuss it in the meantime, and we take it as an agreed fact that he was a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Accepted by the Defence as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before I have formally to give you the possibility of adding some submissions - but only if you so want, of course - let me only summarise one question that personally still concerns me, and this is the question when we come to the question what can we really take into account as mitigating factors. And of course, advantages the accused has already received during the plea agreement can't serve as a mitigating factor. So please, only for my own clarification, is it correct that one advantage was that during the eleven testimonies or statements given to the Prosecution, it was for reasons -- understandable -- it was guaranteed that nothing that he would testify on, no facts he would give to the Prosecution, all this would never be held against him and would never be used for the preparation of an indictment against him? Is this correct that this is one proposal made to him and guarantee given to him? Second, is it correct that when the amendment based on the plea agreement was changed and accepted, that the cumulative conviction or -- all the charges on murder were withdrawn in part as it's in relation to Article 5, intra article 5 -- it's a legal question because it's a question of cumulative convictions. But am I correct in assuming that the charge based on Article 3, murder, was dropped in a give-and-take way as part of the plea agreement? You already explained this morning why and for what purpose not the entire takeover of the Bratunac municipality formed part of this Indictment so that it's limited to Glogova only. And finally, that you stand by your submission. I read carefully once again Mr. Deronjic's testimony in Krstic, that it was not in a give-and-take way as you stated last week, that there was no promise that there would be no indictment in relation to the events in Glogova -- in Srebrenica in 1995. And there's no link between this Indictment, there's no packet solution, including the promise to the accused that he would never be held responsible before this Tribunal based on his participation in the events in Srebrenica in 1995. Are these assumptions correct, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Starting with your latter question, I stand by what I said earlier in respect of Srebrenica 1995 and what I said in respect of the Krstic case. In respect of the first proposition you raised, you said during his eleven testimonies, and what I would like to clarify with Your Honours is the following: When you say "testimonies" do you mean testimonies under oath before the Tribunal or statements to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In respect of the statements that he made to the Office of the Prosecutor, and I think there are nine or ten of them in June and July, there is a memorandum of understanding which has been filed with the Court, and that precisely lays out what the agreement was. So in respect of whether or not when he later testified at a trial under oath, whether he could be prosecuted, of course he could. That's not contained within the memorandum of understanding. But what is understood was when Mr. Deronjic was talking to the Office of the Prosecutor for those ten or eleven sessions, that anything he said would not and could not be used against him. In respect of the Amended Indictment, it was our belief that the persecution count would fully and more completely collect the events and describe the events that took place in Glogova and in -- on that particular day. And that's why we took the larger charge of persecution, and you will see subsumed in the persecution count the various acts that included the burning of personal property, the forcible movement of people, the killings. These are all subsumed in what we consider to be a more serious charge of persecution. And that's why we arrived at the conclusion that persecutions would be a more appropriate count in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. For procedural reasons, I have only -- because we continued with the Sentencing Hearing, I have to give the opportunity, if the parties so want, to give a final statement. Mr. Harmon, do you want to make a final statement or just refer to your previous one?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I would refer to my previous statement. And for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, I led Mr. Deronjic's examination in the Krajisnik case and I am lead counsel in that particular case. I would like to say to Your Honours that the testimony that was provided by Mr. Deronjic in that case, in my opinion, was very solid testimony that was corroborated in many respects by documents, and will be corroborated in the future with other evidence. My conclusion was Mr. Deronjic's testimony was very helpful in illuminating events not only in eastern Bosnia, but to some degree in respect of relationships between people and the way matters were communicated. In addition to which, Mr. Deronjic's testimony was helpful in terms of illuminating as well elements of the joint criminal enterprise; his description, for example, of meetings that took place in Belgrade, and particular in relation to arming, was very helpful. And again, that testimony was corroborated by independent evidence in that particular part of his testimony by a diary that was from an individual by the name of -- as I recall, Mr. Jankovic, who was the head of the SDS in a different municipality. That diary was never seen by Mr. Deronjic before. You know, he was -- he gave the Office of the Prosecutor evidence about the arming and the arming operation and he saw that diary for the first time two or three days before he actually testified in the case. That independent evidence corroborates that there was an arming activity going on. It identified by name, coincidentally, many of the same people who Mr. Deronjic had previously told us were responsible for the arming operation. In addition, in respect of the arming operation, we had an intercept, an intercepted communication between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Kertes, Mr. Kertes being one of the people with whom Mr. Deronjic met I think in late April 1991 along with Mr. Zekic to discuss the arming operation. So in the final analysis, from the Prosecutor's point of view, the testimony of Mr. Deronjic was very, very helpful to us in the Krajisnik case. That's my final submission in this case, Your Honour. Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We thank you. And Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of course abides fully by its closing statement which we made on the 28th of January 2004 during the Sentencing Hearing. In the meantime, nothing has occurred which might influence the standpoint of the Defence, which might change it, and especially not something that might change the proposal made by the Defence as to the sentence that is recommended. Certain inconsistencies and discrepancies in the statements made by the accused, if such discrepancies still exist -- we don't think they do, but if they do, they only confirm his credibility because, like all of us, he is only a human being with only one body and one mind. And he cannot be expected to remember every small detail, the least detail from a time in which events occurred very fast and followed fast on one another's heels. Should the Chamber be in any dilemma, I ask you to apply the old Latin rule in dubio pro reo. This is a simply way for the Trial Chamber to resolve any such doubts by resolving them in favour of the accused. The Chamber should be assured that the accused has not put forward any false facts or evidence, nor has he speculated with the evidence he gave. This Trial Chamber accepted the accused's confession of guilt, the Factual Basis which flesh out his admission of guilt, and of course the Second Amended Indictment because it has already established that all these acts meet the requirements from Rule 62 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. In the view of the Defence, these acts as well as the testimony of Miroslav Deronjic on the 27th of January 2004 before this Trial Chamber can be the only basis and should be the only basis for reaching a decision on the degree of his culpability and the basis for sentencing. However, in the meantime, circumstances have arisen which only go to confirm the view of the Defence and its final submission as to the sentence recommended. The accused, even after the sentencing hearing, continued his substantial cooperation with the Prosecution and the Tribunal by testifying in the case Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. The extent of this testimony and the length of time exceeds all his previous testimonies. It lasted two weeks, and the accused spent over 20 hours altogether in the courtroom. The evidence adduced through the testimony of the accused corroborated, among other things, all his previous testimonies. The scope, quality, and importance of this testimony has already been mentioned by Mr. Mark Harmon, so the Defence will not add anything to this. With his testimony, the accused confirmed his standpoint which is that substantial cooperation is something that he's motivated towards only by the truth. And the accused is still at the disposal of this Tribunal for this reason. The accused, as a witness, was duty-bound to put forward all the facts and all the evidence he knows about. He did this. The facts are what they are, whatever they might mean. Considering that the accused has all the mitigating circumstances that are taken as such in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, we wish to draw attention now to the fact that the substantial cooperation of the accused as the most important mitigating circumstance has only grown in quality and significance with this last testimony. The Defence is even more firmly convinced that even a far milder sentence in the case of this accused would serve to achieve the purpose of punishment in all its essential elements. Therefore, Your Honours, there is nothing else left for me to do but to repeat the final submission of the Defence, which is that in finding the accused guilty the Chamber in our view should not impose a sentence exceeding six years. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank you. Before I have, in the narrowest sense of the word, to give the final word to the accused, I only wanted to come back to one technical issue. It would be of assistance for the preparation of the judgement if the Document S20/A, the A3 aerial view could be brought in a printable version. I know that the Prosecution opposed to the Chamber has these technical possibilities. And therefore, I would appreciate if you could assist us in doing so, but not today, not tomorrow. We have first to write the judgement. I already announced - maybe it was a little bit premature - that the judgement would be handed down the 30th of March. We'll try our very best that we can achieve this in the remaining time. But please don't be surprised if we can't manage it in this period of time. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm informed that the quality of the document that we gave you was the best quality we could produce because it was -- we received only a paper copy of it ourselves. If we have a better copy, of course, we can give you a better copy. But what we had is our initial, large copy. We reproduced, I'm told, the best that we could do. So I'm not sure that we can improve any more on that unless the Defence has at its disposal a better copy they can provide us. And then we will be glad to take this through the necessary steps and get a better copy for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm not that familiarised with the technical possibilities of today, but I was learned that the best way would be to scan the appropriate parts in and have, then, the document in an electronic version and then it could be printed. That's what I learned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm told that we can try, Your Honour. And we will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank you so much. And then, Mr. Deronjic, as it is the final word, do you want to address the Chamber once more, or do you want just to stick to your words you have given to us the last time?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to adhere to my earlier statement. I believe I have nothing to add to it except to thank you and everyone else in the courtroom because you had to invest additional effort in clarifying certain inconsistencies, and I'm sorry that it was due to my mistake that you had to work longer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank you. And I thank everybody for the cooperation today. The trial stays adjourned until further notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: at 2.38 p.m.
